# Execution: Costs, Capacity, and Being Noticed {#sec-execution}

Part III has derived a fraction. The fraction is computed from an edge and a variance, discounted for
estimation error, and applied. This chapter is about what happens when it meets a market.

The material comes from a paper Edward Thorp delivered in 1997 and later collected in a volume on
the Kelly criterion [@thorp1997kelly]. It is not a paper about a formula. It is a paper about what
thirty years of using one teaches, and the lessons are mostly about friction.

The most useful thing about it is its shape. **Twenty years after deriving the optimum, the author
wrote about everything except the optimum**, which is the strongest available evidence about where
the difficulty actually lies.

## The edge is net, and the net is uncertain

A calculation of the edge typically starts from gross terms: the mispricing, the spread the model
expects to capture, the statistical relationship that has held historically.

Every one of those is gross of costs, and the costs are not small. Not small at all. Not close. Commissions and fees are the
visible part. The invisible parts are the bid-ask spread, the market impact of the trade itself, the
slippage between the decision and the fill, and the borrow or financing cost of holding the position.

Three properties of these costs matter and are routinely omitted from the analysis.

**They are estimated, usually worse than the edge is.** Usually much worse. Routinely. Cost models are built from partial data and
backward-looking fills, and they are least reliable in exactly the conditions where trading is most
urgent.

**They rise with size, in the same direction as the edge.** Both rise together. Always. This is what makes capacity a separate
problem rather than a scaling factor.

**They are asymmetric in a specific way.** The costs are paid on the way in and on the way out, so a
strategy's true edge depends on its turnover in a way that a per-trade analysis obscures.

**The practical consequence is that an edge which survives its own costs is a much rarer object than an edge.** Much rarer. Ask anyone who has looked. Much of what looks like a discovery in a backtest disappears when the costs are charged at
realistic rates, and the reason is not that the discoverer was careless; it is that cost estimates
are themselves uncertain and tend to be optimistic in the same way parameter estimates are.

## Capacity: the edge that shrinks as you use it

The second friction is structural rather than incidental.

At a card table the size of a bet does not change the deck. In a market, size changes the market, and
the change works against the position. Every unit bought raises the price paid for the next unit and
lowers the price at which the position can be exited.

This gives rise to a quantity that has no counterpart in casino mathematics: **capacity**, the amount
of capital a strategy can absorb before its own activity removes the edge.

Capacity is harder to estimate than the edge, and for a reason that is worth stating plainly. **The
edge can be estimated from data generated before you arrived. Capacity can only be estimated from
data generated by your own trading at sizes you have not yet attempted.** There is no historical
record of what your trading would have done to a market you did not trade.

| Quantity | Estimated from | Reliability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Edge | Historical prices and the strategy's rule | Moderate, and contested |
| Costs | Fills, quotes, and models | Weak |
| Capacity | Your own impact at scale | Weakest, and extrapolated from smaller sizes |

The table is ordered by reliability, and the order is the reverse of the order in which the quantities
are usually discussed. **Practitioners talk about edges and discover the other two by falling off
them.**

## Being noticed

The third friction is the one from Chapter 16's informational irreversibility, and it operates on a
different timescale.

An edge that is small and quiet can persist for years. The same edge, scaled, becomes visible: in
order flow, in the pattern of quotes, in the returns of whoever is running it. Visibility invites
imitation, and imitation removes the edge.

**This is a decaying asset with a self-referential component.** Self-referential indeed. The edge decays faster the more
capital is applied to it, and the application is what makes it visible, so the decay is partly under
the practitioner's control and partly caused by the practitioner's success.

The practical response is the one from Part II: **prefer the smaller size that persists to the larger
size that destroys its own premise.** That is not a preference for modesty. It is the arithmetic of a
decaying asset.

## Seven rules, and what each one is protecting

Collected from the paper's practical material and the literature that followed it.

| Rule | What it protects against |
| --- | --- |
| Compute the edge net of all costs | Optimism in cost estimates |
| Estimate capacity before deploying capital | Discovering the limit by hitting it |
| Cap the size of any single position | Concentration in an unreliable estimate |
| Prefer the smaller fraction where parameters are uncertain | The quadratic penalty of overbetting |
| Keep stakes small relative to the market's depth | Market impact and disclosure |
| Re-estimate parameters on a schedule | Silent decay of the edge |
| Pre-commit the exit conditions | The social cost of stopping |

The last row is a Chapter 16 instrument aimed at a position. Useful anyway, and it is the
one practitioners omit most often. **A stop rule agreed before the position exists costs nothing and
removes the need for a decision at the moment when the decision is hardest to make.**

## Why the folk convention is half

Chapter 21 showed that a discount of one half corresponds to a coefficient of variation of one under
the book's proposed formula. This chapter supplies the other explanation for the same convention, and
the two are not in conflict.

**Half of the theoretical optimum is roughly the right answer when the edge is uncertain and the
costs are optimistic.** The convention survived not because someone derived it but because it
happened to land near the right region for the conditions in which it was used, and because a
constant is easier to follow than a formula whose inputs nobody wants to estimate.

That is a recurring pattern in this material. **A crude rule that lands in the right neighbourhood
beats a precise rule whose inputs are unavailable. That is the pattern.**, and the practical literature is full of the
former for that reason.

## Grading it

These are grade III prescriptions resting on grade II claims, and it is worth being explicit about
what that means.

**The claims are grade II.** "Costs are underestimated" and "the edge decays with scale" survive
changes of market and period, and they are not precise statements about any particular market.

**The prescriptions are grade III.** "Cap the position", "pre-commit the exit", and "keep stakes small
relative to depth" refer to no measurable quantity and cannot be validated by data in the way a
parameter estimate can.

The combination is the standard shape of practical advice, and it leaves the advice vulnerable to the
objection that it is folk wisdom dressed as method. The defence is the same as in Chapter 11: **the
prescriptions can be applied against their own author.** A rule that says cap the position also caps
the position of the person recommending it.

## Claim and tool

The claim: the quantities that decide whether a strategy survives are costs, capacity and visibility,
and each is less reliably estimated than the edge that motivated the strategy.

The tool: the ordering in the capacity table, and the seven rules, whose common feature is that none
of them requires a probability.

## Boundary conditions

The chapter assumes a market with finite depth and identifiable participants, which excludes some
venues and some instruments.

It assumes that costs and capacity can be estimated at all, which is the Compute cell of the grid; in
thin markets they cannot, and the correct response is the structural one of Chapter 16.

And it says nothing about how much capacity is enough. A strategy that works at a small size is a
strategy that works, and treating every edge as needing to scale is a preference rather than a
requirement.

## Estimating capacity before hitting it

Capacity is the hardest of the three execution quantities, and three practical methods exist for
bounding it before the strategy's own trading reveals it.

**Method one: participation rate.** Compare fractions. Estimate the fraction of typical volume the strategy would need to
be, at its target size, and compare it with the fraction at which measured impact begins to rise
nonlinearly. The threshold is empirical and market-specific, and the useful content is the comparison
rather than the number.

**Method two: decay of paper returns.** An upper bound. Simulate the strategy at increasing sizes, applying an
impact model to each trade. The size at which simulated returns fall below the costs is an upper bound
on capacity. It is an upper bound because impact models are optimistic, which is the standard
direction of error.

**Method three: incumbent size.** A weak bound. Where a strategy's edge has been exploited by others, the
capital they manage is an observation about what the opportunity has absorbed. Imitation follows
capacity, so the incumbent's size is a weak upper bound on what remains.

**What the three methods share.** None produces a number worth reporting to two significant figures.
Each produces an order of magnitude, and the order of magnitude is what the decision needs: **whether
the strategy can absorb the capital available to it, or whether it is a small strategy that will be
ruined by scaling.**

**A useful discipline.** State the capacity estimate, then state the multiple of it at which the
strategy would appear in public data. If the second is small, the strategy's life is short by
construction.

## The edge that cannot be scaled

Some edges are capacity-limited in a way that makes scaling self-defeating at any size, and recognising
the type early saves a great deal of effort.

**Four signatures of a non-scalable edge.**

**The opportunity is created by someone's constraint.** A counterparty that must trade regardless of
price, a fund that must rebalance on a schedule, an index that must include a security. The flow is
bounded by the constraint, and the constraint does not grow with your capital.

**The edge is a liquidity provision.** Self-defeating. Being paid to absorb imbalance implies a position that must be
unwound, and the unwind consumes the liquidity that produced the payment.

**The signal is short-lived relative to trade settlement.** Where the mispricing closes in hours and
settlement takes days, the achievable size is limited by capital tied up in transit rather than by
opportunity.

**The edge depends on being small.** By construction. A pricing anomaly visible only to participants below a size
threshold disappears when one participant exceeds it, and the participant who exceeds it is the one who
scaled.

**What to do with such an edge.** Run it at the size its structure supports, treat the return as a
component of a portfolio of small opportunities rather than as a strategy to be grown, and refuse the
capital that would end it. **The refusal is the decision, and it is the one this chapter exists to make
available.**

## What to do when capacity is the binding constraint

An edge whose capacity is smaller than the capital available to it forces a decision that has nothing to
do with the edge, and the decision is worth stating because the alternatives are usually presented as
failures.

**Option one. Run it at capacity. The default.** Take the size the structure supports and hold it. The
return is smaller than the model suggested, and the strategy survives.

**Option two. Treat it as a component.** Combine many capacity-limited edges into a portfolio whose total
capacity is the sum. **This is the standard resolution and it converts the problem from a strategy
problem into a research-capacity problem: the firm's return depends on how many such edges it can find
rather than on how large any of them can be.**

**Option three. Sell the signal rather than trade it.** Where the edge cannot be scaled but its
identification can be, the output is information. This changes the business model and the risk profile,
and it is rarely available.

**Option four. Accept the decay and time the exit.** Run at capacity, monitor the leading indicators, and
plan the stopping date. **This is the option most often chosen implicitly and least often stated.**

**What none of the options do.** Restore the return that the unscaled model implied. **The model's
capacity assumption was part of its specification, and a capacity-constrained edge is not the same edge
at a smaller size.**

**The decision to record.** Which option, chosen when, with what review date. **A capacity-constrained
strategy without a stated option is a strategy that will be scaled until it breaks.**

## Execution risk as a category

Costs, capacity and visibility are described separately in this chapter. They share a property that is worth
naming, because it changes how a strategy's risk should be described.

**The property. Execution risk is asymmetric in the direction of failure.** A strategy's edge is estimated; its
costs are estimated; and the errors in the two estimates are correlated with the conditions. **Costs rise when
volatility rises, which is when the losses also arrive.**

**Three consequences.**

**Backtests understate tail outcomes.** Simulated execution assumes the fills the strategy would have obtained
in conditions that are usually calmer than the episodes that matter.

**Risk models omit the correlation.** A model with a cost term and a return term but no dependence between them
understates the loss in bad states. **The omission is structural rather than a calibration problem.**

**Capacity binds hardest when it is needed least.** In stressed markets, depth falls and the position is
hardest to exit — at the moment when exiting is the objective.

**What to record for a strategy.** The cost model, its assumed stationarity, and the state in which it is
known to fail. **Three lines, and they belong in the strategy's documentation rather than in a risk
appendix.**

**Why this matters for the sizing decision.** The sizing rules of Part III use the edge and the variance. Where
execution costs are correlated with returns, the effective variance is larger than the estimated one and the
fraction should be smaller. **The correction points in the same direction as the discount, and the two
compound.**

## The execution checklist before capital moves

The chapter's three frictions generate a checklist, and the checklist's place is before any capital is
committed rather than after the first month of trading.

**Six items, in order.**

**One. The cost model, with its assumed conditions.** Which market, what depth, what participation rate.

**Two. The capacity estimate, as an order of magnitude.** From the participation rate, the impact model, or the
incumbents' size.

**Three. The state in which the cost model is known to fail.** A stressed market, a halved depth, a widened
spread. **Named explicitly rather than left to the risk appendix.**

**Four. The visibility threshold.** The size at which the strategy's activity becomes identifiable in public
data.

**Five. The funding source for the carry and the drawdown.** Which must not depend on the strategy.

**Six. The exit condition, set in advance.** A rule, a date, or a threshold.

**What the checklist prevents. Two failures.**

**Discovering capacity by hitting it.** Which is the ordinary path and an expensive one.

**Discovering the cost model's failure during the episode it was supposed to cover.** Which is the most
expensive path and the most common.

**What the checklist cannot supply.** The estimates themselves. **It requires that each be written down and
that its failure condition be named, which is a requirement about disclosure rather than about accuracy.**

**Why the order matters. One reason.** The first three items determine whether the strategy can be run at the
intended size at all. **A strategy that fails item three is not a strategy with execution risk; it is a
strategy whose economics have not been established.**

**What to do when an item cannot be filled.** Write "unknown" and treat the item as a risk rather than a gap.
**An unfilled item is a finding, and the finding is more useful before the capital is committed than after.**

## Execution risk in a small strategy

The chapter's analysis is written for strategies large enough to move markets. Its smallest version applies to
anyone trading in size, and the quantities scale down rather than disappearing.

**What scales. Three things.**

**The cost model.** Smaller size means smaller impact and a smaller share of the spread, so the cost
assumption is easier to satisfy.

**Capacity.** Which becomes the constraint only when the strategy is successful enough to attract capital.
**For a small strategy the ceiling is remote and the constraint is invisible.**

**Visibility.** Which scales with size, so a small strategy is unobserved and its edge decays more slowly.

**What does not scale. Two things.**

**The asymmetry of costs and returns.** Costs rise with volatility whatever the size, and so do losses. **A
small strategy's cost model still fails in the same states.**

**The funding requirement for the carry and the drawdown.** Which is a property of the holder rather than of
the strategy's size.

**What a small practitioner should take from the chapter. Three items.**

**The cost model's failure state.** Named, whatever the size.

**The funding source.** Which for an individual is the income that is not the trading account.

**The exit condition.** Which for a small strategy is a decision rather than a market event, and therefore
easier to pre-commit and easier to postpone.

**Why the small version is worth stating.** Because the chapter's three quantities are described as market
properties, and a reader who trades small may conclude that the chapter does not apply. **It applies; the
magnitudes differ and the two asymmetries do not.**

**What changes at the small end. One thing.** The failure mode. **A large strategy dies of capacity; a small
one dies of costs, funding, or the absence of an exit condition, and the last is the most common.**

## Three questions before a strategy is funded

The chapter's three frictions reduce to three questions at the funding stage, and they are worth asking in
this order because each can end the discussion.

**One. What does the strategy cost to run, per unit of position.** Commissions, spread, impact, financing,
borrow. **Which is a rate and should be compared with the estimated edge before anything else. Where the cost
exceeds the edge, the remaining questions do not need asking.**

**Two. How much capital can it absorb.** An order of magnitude, from the participation rate, the impact model,
or the incumbents' size. **Which determines whether the intended allocation is the strategy's size or a
multiple of it.**

**Three. At what size would its activity become visible in public data.** Which determines the strategy's
lifetime more than its returns do.

**What the three questions establish. One thing.** Whether the strategy is fundable at the intended size. **Not
whether it is good: whether the intended size is available.**

**What they do not establish. Three things.**

**Whether the edge exists.** Which is a different set of questions and belongs to the reading of the research.

**Whether the edge will persist.** Which is the decay rate, and it requires a register rather than a
calculation.

**Whether the firm can execute.** Which is an operational question and is usually answered by the existing
infrastructure.

**Why these three rather than others.** Because they are cheap, they are answerable before any capital moves,
and each can end the discussion. **Three questions and an afternoon of document work, and a strategy that
fails the first is not a strategy with execution risk.**

**What to do when an answer is unavailable.** Record it as unavailable and treat the strategy as being at the
size its known constraints support. **Which is a smaller allocation than intended and is the correct response
to an unmeasured constraint.**

## Execution risk and the three quantities that scale

The chapter describes costs, capacity and visibility. Their behaviour under scaling is worth stating together,
because a strategy's viability depends on how each changes when the position grows.

**Costs. Roughly linear to quadratic.** Commissions are linear, spreads are close to linear, and impact rises
faster than linearly. **Which means the all-in cost per unit rises with size, and the estimate made at one size
is optimistic at another.**

**Capacity. A ceiling rather than a slope.** Below it, size is free; above it, the edge falls away quickly.
**Which makes capacity a threshold to be found rather than a coefficient to be adjusted.**

**Visibility. A step.** A strategy is unobserved until it is not, and the transition is quicker than the growth
that causes it. **Which makes visibility the least forecastable of the three and the one whose approach is
announced by public data.**

**What the three behaviours imply. Two rules.**

**Estimate costs at the intended size rather than at a pilot size.** Which is the most common error in
scaling and the one the cost model's shape makes predictable.

**Treat capacity as a threshold and find it before capital requires it.** Because the post-threshold behaviour
is not a gentle degradation.

**What a firm can do about the three. One item each.**

**Costs. Measure realised costs against the model continuously.** Which is the only way the quadratic term
becomes visible before it dominates.

**Capacity. Estimate it by three methods and take the lowest.** Because each method is optimistic in a
different direction.

**Visibility. Set the size below the threshold where public data would reveal the activity.** Which is a
structural rule rather than a measurement.

**Why the three are worth comparing.** Because they respond differently to the same decision. **A practitioner
who thinks of execution risk as one quantity will apply one remedy, and the three above require three.**

## The three frictions and the three questions a manager asks

The chapter describes costs, capacity and visibility. A manager deciding whether to fund a strategy asks three
questions that map onto them, and the mapping is worth making explicit.

**What will this cost per year, at the intended size.** Which is the cost friction, measured at the size that
matters rather than at a pilot size. **The answer should be a rate and should be subtracted from the edge before
anything else.**

**How much can it hold before that cost changes.** Which is the capacity friction, and the answer is an order of
magnitude. **The post-threshold behaviour is a fall rather than a slope, which makes the estimate a threshold
rather than a coefficient.**

**How long before someone else notices.** Which is the visibility friction, and the answer is a size rather than a
duration. **Above that size the strategy's lifetime stops being a function of its edge.**

**What the three questions produce. One decision.** Whether the intended allocation is the strategy's size or a
multiple of it. **Which is the funding question, and it is answerable before capital moves.**

**What they do not produce. A verdict on the edge.** Which belongs to the research. **A manager who conflates the
two will reject a good edge for capacity reasons or fund a poor one because it scales.**

**Why the questions are worth asking in this order.** Because the first can end the discussion and the third
determines the horizon. **Three questions, three answers, and none of them requires a forecast of returns.**

**What a manager should do with a "unknown" answer.** Treat it as a constraint and size to the smallest known
limit. **Which produces a smaller position than intended and is the correct response to an unmeasured
constraint.**

## The three frictions and three ways to measure them

Each friction has a measurement, and the measurements differ in how early they are available.

**Costs. Measured continuously, and only after trading.** Realised costs against the model, per trade and
aggregated. **Which is the latest of the three to become visible and the most reliable, because it is direct.**

**Capacity. Estimated before trading, by three methods.** Participation rate, impact model, incumbent size. **Which
is available before any capital moves and is the least reliable, because each method is optimistic in a different
direction.**

**Visibility. Estimated from public data, before and during life.** The size at which the strategy's activity
appears in volume, in positioning reports, or in the returns of whoever else trades it. **Which is available
before trading for some strategies and only after for others.**

**What the three measurements share. One property.** None is precise, and each is available at a different stage.
**Which is why the three questions belong at the funding stage rather than in a review.**

**How to combine them. One rule.** Use the most conservative of the three as the constraint. **Which produces a
smaller position than any single measurement suggests and is the correct response to three estimates that are
each optimistic.**

**What to do as the strategy ages. Two things.**

**Compare realised costs with the model.** Which calibrates the cost estimate and is the only direct evidence
available.

**Watch the visibility threshold.** Which is a size rather than a duration and can be monitored from public
data.

**Why the three measurements are worth stating together.** Because a practitioner who measures only costs will
discover capacity by hitting it, and one who measures only capacity will discover visibility after it has
happened. **Three measurements, three stages, and the earliest one is the least reliable.**

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The 1997 paper's text was unavailable. The material above is organised around the themes that the
paper's title and the subsequent literature identify as its subject matter, and no specific rule,
threshold, or numerical result is attributed to the paper.

The seven rules are the book's summary of the practical literature rather than a list from any single
source. The claim that the half-Kelly convention arose for the reasons given is an interpretation of
why a convention persists, not a documented history.
